title: Muslims in Britain
hookLine: a dome in Woking, a terraced house in Liverpool, sailors by the docks in Cardiff

cards: A domed mosque sits behind the trees in Woking, a quiet commuter town south of London. It's named for a woman far away, Shah Jahan, the Begum of Bhopal in India, who helped pay for it.
Up north in Liverpool, a local solicitor named William Quilliam becomes Muslim, takes the name Abdullah, and opens a mosque in a row of ordinary terraced houses.
Down in Cardiff, near the docks, sailors from Yemen and Somalia rent rooms, marry, raise children, and set aside a room to pray. No palace in any of it. Just streets, rain and neighbors.

teach.b: One idea for today: Muslims in Britain are not a single arrival. They are many threads, woven over a long time. Some are converts, like Abdullah Quilliam in Liverpool.
Some are sailors and dock workers, from Yemen, Somalia and the Indian subcontinent, who settled in port towns.
Some are soldiers from India who fought in Britain's wars; near that mosque in Woking there is a burial ground made for Muslim soldiers.
And then came families, from Pakistan, Bangladesh, India and later from Africa, the Middle East and the Balkans, who came to work in mills, factories, hospitals and buses, and stayed.
You can read that history in the buildings. Some mosques were built from the ground up with domes and minarets. Others began as a front room, a shop, a warehouse or an old chapel.
On Brick Lane in East London stands a building put up as a chapel for French Protestant refugees, later a synagogue for Jewish families, and now a mosque.
One building, three faiths, each praying in turn under the same roof.

teach.h: EAST AND WEST BELONG TO GOD.
teach.b: The Qur'an has a line that fits a faith carried to a cold, rainy island: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance."
For British Muslims, that has meant praying in a Cardiff boarding house, a Bradford mill, a Woking garden. The faith didn't wait for the perfect place. It found a corner, faced Mecca, and began.

how: British Muslims pray in a wide range of buildings, from purpose-built mosques to converted houses, shops and chapels, and some local mosques keep and share the history of the people who founded them.

games.q: you live in East London. the old building on your street was a Protestant chapel, then a synagogue. its neighbors change again. what happens to it?
games.why: on Brick Lane, it became a mosque. one roof, three faiths, each praying in turn.

practice: Bring to mind the mosque nearest you, or one you pass on the way to work, and wonder: what was the building before, who prayed there first, how did they find the money, the land, the patience?
Then think of the first handful of people who unrolled their prayer mats in that place. If you pray, ask God's mercy for them in your own words; if not, simply hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Abdullah Quilliam, the Liverpool solicitor who became Muslim and opened one of Britain's first mosques in a row of terraced houses. Today's word.
